Which function answers which question about a model

Source: R/assessment.R
assessment.Rd

Several functions of RiskMap check or assess a model, and each answers a different question. The first questions come before the model is fitted and just after, and the last ones when it is used to predict.

QuestionFunction
Are the data spatially correlated?variogram()
Did the computation of the fit work?check_computation(), and plot_mcmc() and summarise_mcmc() for its samples
How uncertain are the estimates?summary(), profile() and parametric_bootstrap()
Could the model have produced the data?assess_fit()
How well does the model predict, and which of several models predicts better?assess_prediction()
Where do the predictions go beyond what the data support?assess_extrapolation()
How well would the predictions of a model do if the truth were known?assess_simulation()

Details

  • check_computation() is about the computation and not about the model. It says whether the maximum of the likelihood was found, and how large the Monte Carlo error of the estimates is. A wrong model can pass it.

  • assess_fit() compares the data with datasets simulated from the model, to see whether the model misses a feature of them. It says nothing about predictions, and a model that passes is not shown to be right.

  • assess_prediction() leaves observations out, predicts them from the others and scores the predictions, by their sharpness and calibration. It compares models, and the model with the best scores may still miss a feature of the data.

  • assess_extrapolation() needs no outcome at the prediction locations. It shows where their covariates are outside the range of the data and where the data say little about the spatial process.

  • assess_simulation() needs datasets simulated with a known surface, from simulate_glgpm(), and so it is for planning a survey or comparing methods, and not for assessing a fit to data.

The order above is a useful one. A fit whose computation failed shouldn't be assessed further, and the scores of a model that misses a feature of the data are easier to understand when the feature is known.

See also

glgpm(), predict() and simulate_glgpm().
